newsitem.title: UK: BA, American seen behind Virgin/Delta rift.
newsitem.headline: BA, American seen behind Virgin/Delta rift.

text.p: The proposed link-up between British Airways and American Airlines was almost certainly the ultimate cause behind the break-up of a rival transatlantic alliance.
Virgin Atlantic announced on Thursday that it was teaming up with Continental Airlines after two years of sharing codes and aircraft with the much bigger U.S. operator Delta Air Lines.

Delta and Virgin said the parting had been amicable but the news betrayed an industry belief that sooner or later they will have to compete with a BA and American combination, despite fierce lobbying against the deal.

"Our core feeling remains that BA wants to get this deal done and there is no price they will not pay to get it done because it just looks so compelling globally," said an executive with another major airline.

Delta said on Friday the agreement to part had been amicable, although there had been disagreement over the price of the blocks of seats Delta was buying on Virgin's transatlantic flights to London Heathrow.
But Delta now says it was concerned that the link with Virgin could have been a hindrance to getting its own slots at Heathrow, which depends on BA and American getting their deal approved.
"Clearly we have long held aspirations to get in there (Heathrow) in our own right and that's a very major consideration in this," said Michael Medlicott, Delta's vice president for Europe and Asia.
"You do have to consider whether an alliance of this kind will act for or against you in your application for independent slots at Heathrow," he said.

Hitherto Delta has always denied suggestions that it would drop Virgin if it could get its own slots at Heathrow -- something which is only likely to happen if BA and American get their own deal approved.

Meanwhile Virgin has lost no time in finding a new transatlantic partner in Continental. Although Continental is smaller than Delta the Houston-based carrier is regarded as commercially more agile and ensures that Virgin will not be left stranded without a partner should Heathrow be opened up to U.S. carriers.

The move ties a further knot in the growing web of connections between Virgin's owner Richard Branson and Continental's biggest investor and former chairman David Bonderman. Industry sources say the two decided about eight months ago to bring the two airlines together in a transatlantic alliance.

Bonderman's Texas Pacific Group is a key investor in Branson's new British passenger railways operator Virgin Rail Group and backed Branson's Virgin Cinemas venture when it bought the former MGM chain of British cinemas.

In addition the former head of Continental's U.S. domestic commuter airline, Jonathon Ornstein, now runs Branson's Brussels-based Virgin Express airline, while Bonderman recently took a stake in Irish carrier Ryanair.

But Virgin denied suggestions that Bonderman could be invited to take a stake in Branson's main airline Virgin Atlantic, which is currently controlled by Branson's privatley-owned Virgin Travel Group.

"At this stage we have no planbs to sell a stake in Virgin Travel Group," company director Will Whitehorn said. "Yes, it is the case that we have been building a long term business relationship with Texas Pacific Group in other parts of Virgin's business but the deal with Continental made sense in it's own right."

Under the current Anglo-U.S. aviation services treaty only BA, Virgin, American and United Airlines have transatlantic landing rights at Heathrow, the most important European hub for lucrative business travellers.

The British government is making approval of the BA and American deal a condition of reaching an "open skies" air services agreement with the U.S., which in turn would involve giving all U.S. airlines access to Heathrow.

Meanwhile British approval for the deal has been held up by a protracted battle between BA and the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) over a demand that BA give up landing slots at Heathrow to make room for the new competition.
Sooner or later it is believed that agreement will be reached, but nothing is now expected to get done this side of the British election, due by May 22.
"I think now its probably 50/50 whether or not BA and American can get together this summer," said Mike Powell, industry analyst at NatWest Markets.
"But I would say there was a 90 percent chance if you asked me whether they are going to be together by the summer of 1998," he said.
